title: What That CBP Email About Your 10-Day Stay Warning Actually Means
excerpt: US Customs and Border Protection sends automated emails to visitors nearing the end of their authorized stay. Here is what NRIs and temporary visa holders need to know.
body:
• US Customs and Border Protection sends automated email reminders to visitors who have 10 days or fewer remaining on their authorized stay in the United States.
  • The emails come from travelercompliance@cbp.dhs.gov or StayCompliance-DoNotReply@cbp.dhs.gov — any other sender address is likely a phishing scam.
  • The system sometimes sends warnings to travelers who have already left the country, because their departure was not properly recorded in the I-94 database.
  • Travelers can check their admission status and remaining days at i94.cbp.dhs.gov under the "View Compliance" tab.

Travelers in the United States on temporary visas or the Visa Waiver Program have been receiving automated emails from US Customs and Border Protection warning them that their authorized stay is about to expire. The notifications, part of CBP's traveler compliance initiative, have raised questions — and occasional panic — among NRIs, business visitors, and tourists who may not be familiar with the system.

How the System Works

CBP sends email reminders to travelers who have 10 days or fewer remaining on their admission into the United States, according to the agency's official traveler compliance page. The program also sends separate notifications to travelers who may have already overstayed their authorized period.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=IexybXfMLq8

The emails are generated from CBP's I-94 records, which track arrival and departure dates for all non-immigrant visitors. Travelers can independently verify their status on the I-94 website at i94.cbp.dhs.gov by clicking the "View Compliance" tab and entering their name, date of birth, and passport number.

CBP has emphasized that the email program does not represent any change in enforcement policy. "This proactive approach only changes how transparent CBP's work is to the traveling public, and helps ensure the public stays in compliance with their terms of admission," the agency stated.

"Travelers can independently verify their status on the I-94 website at i94.cbp.dhs.gov by clicking the "View Compliance" tab and entering their name, date of birth, and passport number."

Watch for Phishing Scams

Legitimate notifications come exclusively from travelercompliance@cbp.dhs.gov or StayCompliance-DoNotReply@cbp.dhs.gov. CBP has warned travelers that any email from a different address claiming to be a stay compliance notice could be a phishing attempt. Travelers should not click links or provide personal information in response to suspicious emails.

The safest course of action is to navigate directly to i94.cbp.dhs.gov to check your compliance status rather than clicking links in any email, even if it appears legitimate.

Why You Might Get a Warning After Leaving

Multiple travelers on forums such as TripAdvisor and Australian Frequent Flyer have reported receiving 10-day warnings despite having departed the United States weeks or months earlier. The issue stems from incomplete departure records in the I-94 database.

The I-94 system depends on airlines and ports of exit to report departure data. If a traveler's departure is not recorded — a known gap in the system — CBP's automated tool treats them as still present in the country and triggers the warning email.

This is more than a bureaucratic annoyance. A missing departure record can flag a traveler as having overstayed, potentially jeopardizing future ESTA applications or visa renewals.

What to Do If Your Record Is Wrong

Travelers who receive an erroneous warning should take immediate steps to correct their I-94 record. CBP offers a contact form at help.cbp.gov where travelers can select "I94 travel compliance" as the topic and "10 day notification email" as the applicable issue. According to forum accounts, CBP has been responsive, often replying within the same day.

Travelers should also keep boarding passes, airline confirmation emails, or bank statements showing transactions in their home country on the date of departure. These documents can serve as proof if CBP needs to verify an exit.

What NRIs Need to Know

For Indian nationals visiting the US on B-1/B-2 visas or other temporary categories, the 10-day warning is a reminder that overstaying — even by a single day — can have serious consequences. An overstay of more than 180 days triggers a three-year bar on re-entry, while staying beyond 365 days results in a 10-year bar under US immigration law.

The compliance check feature at i94.cbp.dhs.gov is available to travelers admitted under most classes of admission. Immigration attorneys recommend checking the I-94 record within days of arriving in the US to confirm that the correct admit-until date has been recorded, rather than waiting for a warning email that may or may not arrive.

For additional questions, travelers can contact CBP's Traveler Communications Center at (202) 325-8000 or visit the I-94 FAQ page for guidance.
nri_angle: Indian visitors to the US on B-1/B-2 visas should understand CBP's automated stay compliance emails and check their I-94 records to avoid overstay issues.
